The FBI in the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor's Office investigated dozens of East Cleveland officers. And in some cases, the inquiry had unforeseen consequences. The acting police chief, Kenneth Lundy, was eventually. fired, resulting in a reevaluation of cases he had worked on, including the case of Jerry Sims Jr., a convicted murderer. In 2025, Lundy was named in a petition for a new trial for Sims, who had been found guilty of aggravated murder in 2019 and was serving 40 years to life. Lundy had been the lead detective on Jerry Sims' case, but was now accused of inappropriate conduct during the investigation and trial. According to the petition, Lundy used his position. as a detective to initiate a manipulative and exploitative relationship with the key witness whose testimony resulted in Jerry Sims' conviction. The witness now claimed Lundy pressured her into providing false testimony, and then harassed and intimidated her. With this new information and following an evidentiary hearing, the charges against Jerry Sims Jr. were dismissed, and he was released from prison. Lundy wasn't the only one to face the consequences of his actions. Detective Ian McKinnis, who was filmed kicking multiple suspects, was found guilty of a multitude of charges, including assault, dereliction of duty, and interfering with civil rights, and sentenced to two and a half years in prison. Sergeant Anthony Holmes pled guilty to attempted telecommunications fraud and was sentenced to 180 days in prison. However, he's currently appealing his sentence. Commander Larry McDonald was convicted of tampering with records, two counts of obstructing official business, dereliction of duty, tampering with evidence, and telecommunications fraud, and sentenced to four years in prison. All three must permanently surrender their law enforcement licenses. In total, 16 East Cleveland Police officers have been indicted or accused of committing various offenses, including assault, falsification, dereliction of duty, interfering with civil rights, obstructing official business, telecommunications fraud, theft during traffic stops, vandalism, money laundering, tampering with records, insurance fraud, bribery, or disorderly conduct, and several have faced a range of punishments from community control, probation, prison time, or the surrender of their law enforcement licenses. The FBI in the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor's Office investigated dozens of East Cleveland officers.
And in some cases, the inquiry had unforeseen consequences.
The acting police chief, Kenneth Lundy, was eventually.
fired, resulting in a reevaluation of cases he had worked on, including the case of Jerry Sims Jr., a
convicted murderer. In 2025, Lundy was named in a petition for a new trial for Sims, who had been
found guilty of aggravated murder in 2019 and was serving 40 years to life. Lundy had been the
lead detective on Jerry Sims' case, but was now accused of inappropriate conduct during the
investigation and trial. According to the petition, Lundy used his position.
as a detective to initiate a manipulative and exploitative relationship with the key witness
whose testimony resulted in Jerry Sims' conviction. The witness now claimed Lundy pressured her
into providing false testimony, and then harassed and intimidated her. With this new information
and following an evidentiary hearing, the charges against Jerry Sims Jr. were dismissed, and he was
released from prison. Lundy wasn't the only one to face the consequences of his actions. Detective Ian
McKinnis, who was filmed kicking multiple suspects, was found guilty of a multitude of charges,
including assault, dereliction of duty, and interfering with civil rights, and sentenced to two
and a half years in prison. Sergeant Anthony Holmes pled guilty to attempted telecommunications fraud
and was sentenced to 180 days in prison. However, he's currently appealing his sentence.
Commander Larry McDonald was convicted of tampering with records, two counts of obstructing
official business, dereliction of duty, tampering with evidence, and telecommunications fraud,
and sentenced to four years in prison. All three must permanently surrender their law enforcement licenses.
In total, 16 East Cleveland Police officers have been indicted or accused of committing various
offenses, including assault, falsification, dereliction of duty, interfering with civil rights,
obstructing official business, telecommunications fraud, theft during traffic stops,
vandalism, money laundering, tampering with records, insurance fraud, bribery, or disorderly conduct,
and several have faced a range of punishments from community control, probation, prison time,
or the surrender of their law enforcement licenses.
